title: A new plant species from the Abo Formation, early Permian (Leonardian), of New Mexico, a colonizer of disturbed habitats with implications regarding rarity in the fossil record
content:
Abstract
Background and Aims
Fossil plant rarity in the geological record may be a consequence of original rarity, preservational biases resulting from habitat preference or susceptibility to decay, or collector biases. Rarity of suspected colonizers is particularly interesting, especially if the inferred environment was one of frequent disturbances. This is magnified for strata that have been highly prospected and have produced many fossils. Here, a previously unknown, small, colonizing plant is described from the early Permian Abo Formation, New Mexico, USA. We describe this plant and its ecological dimensions.
Methods
The plant remains were located by surface prospecting outcrops of the Abo Formation in Socorro County, New Mexico. Remains were examined microscopically and photographed at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science using standard photographic equipment and lighting techniques.
Key Results
The plant remains were previously unknown and are described here as representing a new genus and species. Plant habit is upright, centrally rooted, bearing numerous singly compound leaves, clustered at the apex. Stems are ∼5 mm in diameter. Heights, including the crown, are estimated to be about 20 cm. Other than being a tracheophyte, the affinity of the plant is uncertain above the level of genus. It is probably a seed plant, but other affinities are possible; no reproductive organs were found. Stem bases are crowded on a bedding-plane surface interpreted to have formed in a sheet flood. The plants were buried in a subsequent flood.
Conclusions
The new species was a colonizer of disturbed habitats. The density of the stems, their upright habit and the environment suggest a seed-plant affinity. Its rarity is puzzling given its inferred ecology and the decades of palaeontological prospecting of the Abo Formation (and its northern and southern equivalents), which otherwise has uncovered numerous plant, animal, and ichnological remains.
